## Q1
Arrange the following events in the correct order when an interrupt occurs during instruction execution.<br>
A. Save program counter (PC) and status register<br>
B. Fetch interrupt vector from memory<br>
C. Execute the interrupted instruction completely<br>
D. Transfer control to interrupt service routine (ISR)<br>
E. Restore PC and register after ISR

## Q1 - Options
(A) A, B, C, D, E
(B) E, D, C, B, A
(C) C, A, B, D, E
(D) A, B, E, C, D

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Interrupts, DMA, Instruction Cycle & Addressing Modes
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q49

An interrupt is only acted on at an instruction boundary, and the processor then follows a fixed save-dispatch-restore sequence.

C, A, B, D, E.

- **C. Execute the interrupted instruction completely** — the processor finishes the instruction already in progress before reacting to the interrupt.
- **A. Save program counter (PC) and status register** — the context is saved so the interrupted program can be restored later.
- **B. Fetch interrupt vector from memory** — the processor locates the address of the appropriate interrupt service routine.
- **D. Transfer control to interrupt service routine (ISR)** — execution jumps to that routine.
- **E. Restore PC and register after ISR** — once the ISR finishes, the saved PC and status register are restored so normal execution can resume.

## Q2
Which of the following are characteristics of RISC architecture?

A. Large instruction set with many adversing modes<br>
B. Fixed instruction length<br>
C. Emphasis on software rather than hardware<br>
D. Simple instruction that execute in one cycle

## Q2 - Options
(A) A, B Only
(B) B, C, D Only
(C) A, C, D only
(D) A, B, C, D

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Interrupts, DMA, Instruction Cycle & Addressing Modes
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q52

RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) design keeps the hardware simple and pushes complexity into the compiler, which is the opposite philosophy of CISC.

- **A. Large instruction set with many adversing modes** — this describes CISC, not RISC. RISC deliberately keeps the instruction set small with few addressing modes so the hardware stays simple.
- **B. Fixed instruction length** — correct. RISC instructions are uniform in length so they can be fetched and decoded quickly in a pipeline.
- **C. Emphasis on software rather than hardware** — correct. RISC shifts complexity to the compiler, letting the hardware stay minimal.
- **D. Simple instruction that execute in one cycle** — correct. Most RISC instructions are designed to complete in a single clock cycle to support efficient pipelining.

Only B, C and D describe RISC, so the answer is B, C, D only.

## Q3
Based on the passage, how much CPU time is consumed by programmed I/O?

A system transfers data blocks of 2000 bytes.

With programmed I/O, each byte transfer takes 6 CPU cycles.<br>
With direct memory access (DMA), the block transfer takes 3000 cycles in total for the DMA controller, in addition to a CPU setup overhead of 200 cycles.<br>
The CPU clock speed is 1 GHz, so one clock cycle equals 1 nanosecond.

## Q3 - Options
(A) 12 μs
(B) 20 μs
(C) 24 μs
(D) 30 μs

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Interrupts, DMA, Instruction Cycle & Addressing Modes
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q96

Programmed I/O keeps the CPU busy for every single byte of the transfer, so the total CPU cycles must be computed first and then converted to time using the clock speed.

CPU cycles = 2000 bytes × 6 cycles/byte = 12,000 cycles<br>
CPU time = 12,000 cycles / 1 GHz = 12,000 nanoseconds = 12 microseconds

12 microseconds is the CPU time consumed by programmed I/O.

## Q4
Based on the passage, which approach is more CPU-efficient for large block transfers?

A system transfers data blocks of 2000 bytes.

With programmed I/O, each byte transfer takes 6 CPU cycles.<br>
With direct memory access (DMA), the block transfer takes 3000 cycles in total for the DMA controller, in addition to a CPU setup overhead of 200 cycles.<br>
The CPU clock speed is 1 GHz, so one clock cycle equals 1 nanosecond.

## Q4 - Options
(A) Programmed I/O
(B) DMA
(C) Both programmed I/O and DMA
(D) Depends on block size

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Interrupts, DMA, Instruction Cycle & Addressing Modes
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q97

DMA is designed to free the CPU from handling each byte of a transfer individually. The DMA controller moves the entire block on its own, and the CPU only pays a brief 200-cycle setup cost, compared with 12,000 cycles of CPU involvement under programmed I/O for the same 2000-byte block.

Because the CPU is occupied for far fewer cycles with DMA, DMA is the more CPU-efficient approach for large block transfers.

## Q5
Based on the passage, how many CPU cycles are spent with DMA?

A system transfers data blocks of 2000 bytes.

With programmed I/O, each byte transfer takes 6 CPU cycles.<br>
With direct memory access (DMA), the block transfer takes 3000 cycles in total for the DMA controller, in addition to a CPU setup overhead of 200 cycles.<br>

## Q5 - Options
(A) 200 Cycles
(B) 3000 Cycles
(C) 3200 Cycles
(D) 4000 Cycles

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Interrupts, DMA, Instruction Cycle & Addressing Modes
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q98

With DMA, the CPU only performs the initial setup work and then hands off the actual byte-by-byte transfer to the DMA controller entirely. The 3000 cycles described for the block transfer are the DMA controller's own bus cycles for moving the data, not CPU cycles, so they do not count against the CPU's workload.

CPU cycles spent with DMA = 200 cycles (setup overhead only)

The CPU is occupied for only the 200-cycle setup overhead while DMA handles the transfer.

## Q9 - Options
(A) A, B, C, D, E
(B) B, A, D, A, E
(C) B, C, A, D, E
(D) C, B, A, D, E

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Interrupts, DMA, Instruction Cycle & Addressing Modes
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q41

The processor must first fetch the instruction and decode it to know its addressing mode. It can then calculate the effective address, fetch the needed operands, and execute the operation. That order is B, C, A, D, E.

**Answer:** A

**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2025 (26 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q43

## Q15
Consider the following statement regarding special purpose registers.<br>
A. Program Counter (PC) keeps the track of next instruction executed<br>
B. Instruction register holds the address of first instruction to be executed<br>
C. Accumulator holds the output of ALU<br>
D. Program Counter ( PC ) keeps the track of only first instruction of the program

## Q15 - Options
(A) (A) and (C) Only
(B) (A) and (D) Only
(C) (B) and (D) Only
(D) (A), (B) and (C) Only

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Interrupts, DMA, Instruction Cycle & Addressing Modes
**Source:** UGC NET Aug 2024 (23 Aug, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q82

(A) is true — the program counter holds the address of the next instruction to be executed. (C) is true — the accumulator holds the ALU’s result. (B) is false: the instruction register holds the instruction currently being executed, not an address. (D) is false: the PC tracks the next instruction throughout execution, not only the first. Only (A) and (C) — option A.
